It is reported that Ibn Mas'ud used to recite it as: "yad'u man darruhu aqrabu min naf'ihi" (he calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit).

The scholars of Arabic differed regarding the position of "man" (min). Some of the grammarians of Basra said: its position is in the accusative, governed by "yad'u" (calls upon), and he said its meaning is: he calls upon gods whose harm is nearer than their benefit. He said: it is anomalous, because it is not found in speech: "yad'u li-Zaydan" (he calls upon for Zayd). Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: the lam is part of the relative complement of "ma" after "man", as if the meaning of the sentence in his view is: he calls upon the one for whose harm is nearer than his benefit. It is related from the Arabs, by hearing from them, in my opinion: "lama ghayruhu khayrun minhu" (what belongs to another is better than it), meaning: "ʿindi ma li-ghayrihi khayrun minhu" (with me, what belongs to another is better than it), and "a'taytuka lima ghayruhu khayrun minhu," meaning: "ma li-ghayrihi khayrun minhu." He said: it is permissible in everything in which the case is not clearly shown to interpose the lam, not the noun.

Others among them said: it is permissible that the meaning of that be: "huwa al-dalal al-ba'id yad'u" (it is the far error that he calls upon), so that "yad'u" is the relative clause of "al-dalal al-ba'id", and the pronoun is implied in "yad'u", then one resumes the sentence with the lam, saying of "li-man darruhu aqrabu min naf'ihi": "labi'sa al-mawla" (wretched is the protector), like your saying in conditional style: "lama fa'altu lahuwa khayrun laka" (what you did is indeed better for you). According to this view, "man" is in the nominative position by the pronoun in His words "darruhu" (its harm), because "man", when it is a conditional, is case-marked by what follows it; and the second lam in "labi'sa al-mawla" is the response to the first lam. This latter view is more correct according to the school of Arabic grammar, while the first is closer to the school of the interpreters.

* *

As for His words ﴿labi'sa al-mawla (Wretched is the protector)﴾:

He says: wretched is this cousin (ibn al-ʿamm), the one who worships God on an edge.

﴿wa-labi'sa al-ʿashir (and wretched is the companion)﴾: he says: and wretched is the associate who lives with him, and the companion; he is:

As related:

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿and wretched is the companion﴾: the ʿashir is the one who keeps company, the companion.

It has been said that by "al-mawla" in this place is meant the ally and helper.

Mujahid used to say: by His words ﴿wretched is the protector, and wretched is the companion﴾ is meant the idol (al-wathan).

⁕ Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God ﴿and wretched is the companion﴾, he said: the idol.

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil, meaning explanation) of His words, exalted is He:** ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾ (14)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Indeed, Allah will admit those who affirmed Allah and His Messenger, acted upon what Allah commanded them in the world, and refrained from what He forbade them in it, into gardens, meaning orchards, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾. He says: the rivers flow from beneath their trees. ﴿Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills﴾: so He gives to the people of His obedience from His honour whatever He wishes, and inflicts humiliation on the people of His disobedience as He wishes.

* *

**The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:** ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not give him victory in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky and then cut it off, and see whether his scheme removes that which enrages him.﴾ (15)

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil, meaning explanation) of His words, exalted is He:** ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾ (14)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Indeed, Allah will admit those who affirmed Allah and His Messenger, acted upon what Allah commanded them in the world, and refrained from what He forbade them in it, into gardens, meaning orchards, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾. He says: the rivers flow from beneath their trees. ﴿Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills﴾: so He gives to the people of His obedience from His honour whatever He wishes, and inflicts humiliation on the people of His disobedience as He wishes.

* *

**The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:** ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not give him victory in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky and then cut it off, and see whether his scheme removes that which enrages him.﴾ (15)

On the interpretation of His words, "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him (the Prophet) in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky, then cut it off and see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him" (22:15) and "Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, and [know that] Allah guides whom He wills" (22:16):

The exegetes differed concerning the referent of the pronoun in His words, "that Allah will never help him" (an yanṣurahu Allāh).

Some said: it refers to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). According to the interpretation of some of those who held this view: "Whoever among the people thinks that Allah will never help Muhammad in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope, which is the sabab (cord, means), to the sky," meaning the sky of the House (the Ka'bah), that is its roof, "then let him cut it off" after he has strangled himself with it. "Then let him see whether his strangling removes that which enrages him." And by "cutting it off after the strangling" is meant: "whether that removes what enrages him," i.e., whether it removes from his breast the rage he feels.

Mention of those who said this:

- Naṣr b. ʿAlī narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: Khālid b. Qays narrated to me, from Qatādah: "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help His Prophet, nor his religion, nor his Book, *then let him stretch a cord* (fa-l-yamdud bi-sabab)," he says: with a rope to the sky of the House, "and let him strangle himself with it," *"then let him see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him."*

- Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Muhammad b. Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah: "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him in this world and the Hereafter," he said: whoever thinks that Allah will never help His Prophet (ﷺ). "Then let him stretch a cord," he says: with a rope to the sky of the House. "Then let him cut it off," he says: then let him strangle himself; then let him see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him.

- al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah, similarly.

Others who said that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to the mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that "the sky" mentioned in this passage is the well-known sky, said:

The meaning of the speech is:

- Yūnus narrated this to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words, "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him in this world and the Hereafter," and he recited up to "whether his scheming removes that which enrages him," and said: whoever thinks that Allah will never help His Prophet (ﷺ), and strives against this matter to cut it off from him, then let him cut that off at its root, from where it comes to him. For its root is in the sky. So let him stretch a cord to the sky, and then cut off from the Prophet (ﷺ) the revelation that comes to him from Allah, for he will not be able to plot against it until its root is cut off from him. So he schemed to cut off its root from him. "Then let him see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him": that which has entered them of this, and that which Allah has enraged them with, of the support of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of what is sent down upon him.

Others who said that the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ) said: the meaning of "naṣr" here is provision (rizq). According to the view of these, the interpretation of the speech is: whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for Muhammad in this world, and will not give him, [let him ...]. They also mentioned an attested usage from the Arabs: "Whoever helps me, Allah helps him," meaning: whoever gives me, Allah gives him. And they also related an attested usage from them: "The rain helped (naṣara) the land of such-and-such," when it soaked it and gave it life.

As evidence for this they cited the verse of al-Fuqaʿsī:

"Indeed you do not give a man beyond his portion, nor do you possess the cleft which the rain helps (al-ghayth nāṣiruhu)."

[The verse is by al-Fuqaʿsī, as the author said. The point of citation is his words "al-ghayth nāṣiruhu." In Lisān al-ʿArab (root n-ṣ-r) it is said: Abū Ḥanīfa al-Dīnawarī said: al-nāṣir and al-nāṣira are what comes from a distant place to the valley, so the floods "help" (naṣr al-sayl). "Naṣara al-bilād yanṣuruhā" means he came to it. From Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "Naṣarat arḍ Banī fulān" means I came to it. "Naṣara al-ghayth al-arḍ naṣran" means it aided, watered and made it grow. He said: "Whoever was missed by the spring, then only the Ḥijāz is helped by the rain of ʿAbd al-Wāḥid." And "naṣara al-ghayth al-balad" means when it helps it toward fertility and vegetation. Abū ʿUbayda said: "Nuṣirat al-bilād" means when it has been rained upon, so it is manṣūra, that is, mamṭūra. "Naṣara al-qawm" means when they were given rain. And in a hadith: "Indeed this cloud helps the land of Banū Kaʿb," meaning it rains upon them.]

Mention of those who said this:

- Abū Kurayb narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah narrated to us, saying: Isrāʾīl narrated to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Tamīmī, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbās: "Tell me about His words, 'Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a cord to the sky, then cut it off and see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him.'" He said: whoever thinks that Allah will never help Muhammad, let him tie a rope to a roof, then strangle himself with it until he dies.

- Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Ḥakkām narrated to us, from ʿAnbasa, from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdānī, from al-Tamīmī, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbās about His words, "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him." He said: that Allah will never provide for him in this world and the Hereafter. "Let him stretch a cord to the sky": the cord is the rope, and the sky is the roof of the House; let him hang a rope from the roof of the House, then let him strangle himself. "Then let him see whether his scheming removes" this which he has done of the rage he feels.

- Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Ḥakkām narrated to us, from ʿAmr b. Muṭarrif, from Abū Isḥāq, from a man of Banū Tamīm, from Ibn ʿAbbās, similarly.

- Muḥammad b. Bashshār narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Tamīmī, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a cord to the sky," he said: the sky of the House.

- Muḥammad b. al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Abū Dāwūd narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: I heard al-Tamīmī say: I asked Ibn ʿAbbās, and he mentioned something similar.

- Muḥammad b. Saʿd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words, "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him in this world and the Hereafter ... up to His words, 'that which enrages him'": He said: the sky to which Allah commanded that a cord be stretched is the roof of the House; He commanded that a rope be stretched to it, and that he strangle himself with it. He said: "Then let him see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him," when he strangles himself, if he fears that Allah will not help him!

Others said: the pronoun in "yanṣuruhu" refers to "man" (whoever). They said: the meaning of the speech is: whoever thinks that Allah will never provide for him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a cord to the sky of the House, then strangle himself; then let him see whether his act removes that which enrages him, namely that he is not provided for!

Mention of those who said this:

- Muḥammad b. ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me [[There is an abbreviation in the chain, perhaps by the copyist.]], from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, concerning the saying of Allah, "that Allah will never help him": he said: Allah will provide for him. "Then let him stretch a cord" he said: with a rope; "to the sky" the sky above you; "then let him cut it off" that is, let him strangle himself; whether his scheming, that strangling, removes that he will not be provided for.

- al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, concerning His words, "Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him": Allah provides for him; "let him stretch a cord to the sky": with a rope to the sky.

Ibn Jurayj said, from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "to the sky" means to the sky of the House. Ibn Jurayj said: Mujāhid said: "Then let him cut it off" means let him strangle himself, and that is his scheming, "that which enrages him": that strangling is that Allah will not provide for him.

- I was told by al-Ḥusayn, who said: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd b. Sulaymān narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say, concerning His words, "then let him stretch a cord" meaning: with a rope, "to the sky" meaning: the sky of the House.

- Yaʿqūb narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah narrated to us, saying: Abū Rajāʾ informed us, saying: ʿIkrimah was asked about His words, "then let him stretch a cord to the sky," and he said: the sky of the House. "Then let him cut it off": he said: let him strangle himself.

The most correct interpretation of this, in my view, is the view of those who said that the pronoun refers to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and his religion. This is because Allah, exalted is His mention, mentioned a people who worship Him "on an edge": they are content with the religion if they obtain good in their worship of Him, and they turn back from their religion when a hardship afflicts them in it. Then He followed this with this verse. It is known that He only followed it with it as a rebuke to them for their apostasy from the religion, or for their doubt in it, their hypocrisy, their slowness in seeking breadth in livelihood or abundance in provision. Since the requirement is that this be consequent upon the report about their hypocrisy, the meaning of the speech then, given that it is so, is: whoever thinks that Allah will not provide for Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community in this world, so that He would not expand His bounty upon them in it, and would not provide for them in the Hereafter with the bright gifts of His generosity and honour, out of impatience with Allah's doing that to him and to them, then let him stretch a cord to a sky above him, whether a roof of a house or something else to which the cord may be hung from above, then let him strangle himself when he is enraged at some of what Allah has decreed, hastening the removal of that from him. Then let him see whether his scheming, his strangling in this way, removes that which enrages him. If that does not remove his rage until Allah brings relief from Him and removes it, then likewise his hastening of Allah's help for Muhammad and his religion will not delay what Allah has decreed for him of that beyond its appointed time, nor hasten it before its time.

It is related that this verse was revealed concerning Asad and Ghaṭafān, who were slow to embrace Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and so the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will neither supply us with food nor give us water." So Allah, blessed and exalted, said to them: whoever hastens Allah's help for Muhammad, let him stretch a cord to the sky and strangle himself; let him see whether his hastening by that removes his rage. Likewise his hastening of Allah's help for Muhammad, when His help has not been advanced before its time.

The grammarians differed concerning the "mā" in His words, "that which enrages him" (mā yaghīẓ). Some of the grammarians of Basra said it has the meaning of "alladhī" (which), and said: the meaning of the speech is "whether his scheming removes that which enrages him"; he said the pronoun was omitted because it is the connecting element of "alladhī," since when the two become one noun, omission is lighter. Another said: rather, it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) which has no need of a pronoun: "whether his scheming removes his rage."

* *

As for His words, "Thus We have sent it down as clear signs":

He, exalted is His mention, says: Just as I have made My proofs clear to you concerning the one who denies My power to bring back to life those of creation who have died after their extinction, having made them plain, O people, so We have sent down to Our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) this Qur'an as clear signs, meaning manifest proofs, which guide to the truth whom Allah wills to guide. "And [know that] Allah guides whom He wills": He, may His praise be exalted, says: and because Allah guides to what is right and to the path of truth whomever He wills, He sent down this Qur'an as clear signs. Here "anna" (that) is in the accusative position.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 22, verse 17:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with Allah — indeed Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, the separation between these hypocrites who worship Allah with a condition (ʿalā ḥarf), and those who associated others with Allah, worshipping idols and images, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians, and the Magians, who venerate and serve the fires, and between those who believe in Allah and His messengers, is toward Allah. He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection with a just decision, and His separating them is by admitting into the Fire all the factions, and into the Garden the believers in Him and His messengers. That is the separation from Allah between them.

Qatadah used to say concerning this:

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with Allah﴾ He said: The Sabeans are a people who worship the angels, pray toward the qiblah, and recite the Psalms (al-Zabur). The Magians worship the sun, the moon, and the fires. Those who associate others with Allah worship idols. The religions are six: five for Satan, and one for the Most Merciful.

"Inna" was introduced into the predicate of the first "inna" because of the meaning I have mentioned, and because the speech carries the sense of a conditional, as if it were said: whoever is upon one of these religions, then Allah will separate what is between him and whoever opposes him. The Arabs sometimes introduce "inna" into the predicate of "inna" when the predicate of the first noun is a noun attached to a pronoun referring back to it. So you say: "Indeed ʿAbd Allah, indeed the good is abundant with him," as the poet said:

*Indeed the caliph — indeed Allah has clothed him*
*With the garment of kingship, by which the outcomes are hoped for.*

[The verse is by Jarir (from his Diwan, al-Sawi edition, p. 527), from a qasidah praising some of the Banu Marwan. In his transmission, "yakfi" stands in place of the first "inna." "Turja" stands in place of "turjā" [i.e., "tuzjā"]. The commentator of the Shawahid al-Kashshaf said: "The outcome (khatim) of a thing is its consequence, and tuzjā means are driven; the outcomes of command. The khatim, with the taʾ open or closed, is said; one says azjaytu al-ibil, meaning I drove the camels." The verse is cited as evidence at the words of the Exalted, "Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans... indeed Allah will judge between them": "inna" was introduced upon each of the two parts of the sentence, for added emphasis. The entrance of the second "inna" upon the clause functioning as predicate is justified by the lengthy separation between them by the conjunctions. The author cited the verse as evidence that it is analogous to what occurs in the Qur'anic verse, the introduction of the second "inna" upon a predicate clause containing a pronoun. The verse admits another possibility, namely that the clause "inna Allah sarbalahu sirbal mulk" is a parenthetical clause between the subject of "inna" and its predicate; this is not permissible in the verse, as said by Abu Hayyan, who transmitted it from the commentator of the Shawahid al-Kashshaf. End. "Al-sirbal" means the shirt or the coat of mail, and what is meant here is the first.]

Al-Farra' used to say: Whoever says this does not say "innaka innaka qa'im," nor "inna iyyaka innahu qa'im," because the two nouns differ; so the rejection of the first is good, and the second is treated as if it were the subject. It is good because of the difference and disliked because of the sameness.

* *

As for His words: ﴿Indeed Allah is, over all things, Witness﴾

He says: Indeed Allah is witness over every thing of the deeds of these categories that Allah, mighty is His praise, has mentioned, and over other things as well, all of them; nothing of that is hidden from Him.

**The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many of mankind? But many deserve the punishment.﴾**

He, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ):

Have you not seen, O Muhammad, with your heart, so that you know that God is prostrated to by whoever is in the heavens, from among the angels, and whoever is on the earth, from among creation, from among the jinn and others, and the sun, the moon, and the stars in the sky, and the mountains, and the trees, and the creatures on the earth? The prostration of these is their shadows, when the sun rises upon them and when it declines. Whenever the shadow of anything shifts, that is its prostration.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾, he said: "These are all shadows."

As for the prostration of the sun, the moon and the stars, it is as follows.

As related:

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi ʿAdiyy and Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, the two of them saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu al-ʿAliyah al-Riyahi say: "There is no star in the sky, nor sun, nor moon, but it falls prostrate before God when it sets. Then it does not move until it is permitted, and it takes its course to the right." Muhammad added: "until it returns to its place of rising."

* *

And His words: ﴿and many of mankind﴾

He says: many of the children of Adam prostrate, and they are the believers in God.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿and many of mankind﴾, he said: "The believers."

* *

And His words: ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾

He, the Exalted, says: many of the children of Adam deserve the punishment of God, and it is incumbent upon them because of their disbelief in Him, yet even so their shadows prostrate to God.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾, and "they prostrate along with their shadows." Thus, according to this interpretation that we have mentioned from Mujahid, the words ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿and many of mankind﴾, and it is included among those whom God described as prostrating to Him, and His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾ are a complement of "many." If the second "many" referred to those not included among those described as prostrating, it would be in the nominative case governed by the pronoun referring back to it in His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾, and the meaning of the statement would then be: "and many refused prostration," because His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾ indicate disobedience to God and refusal to prostrate, for which they deserved punishment.

18

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Whomever God humiliates, there is none to honor him. Indeed God does what He wills﴾ (17)

He, the Exalted, says: Whomever God humiliates among His creation, and so makes him wretched, ﴿there is none to honor him﴾ with happiness, by which He makes him happy, because all affairs are in the hand of God. He grants success to whom He wills in obedience to Him, forsakes whom He wills, makes wretched whom He intends, and makes happy whom He loves.

* *

And His words: ﴿Indeed God does what He wills﴾

He, the Exalted, says: Indeed God does what He wills among His creation, humiliating whom He wills to humiliate and honoring whom He wills to honor, because the creation is His creation and the command is His command. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾. It has been reported that some of them recited it as ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ مُكْرَمٍ﴾ (fa-ma lahu min mukramin, with the fatha on the mim of mukram), meaning: "there is none to give him honor." But that is a recitation I do not consider permissible, because of the consensus (ijma') of the authorities among the reciters against it.

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads. With it, what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted. And for them are hooks of iron. Every time they wish to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it, and [they will be told], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ (19–22)

The interpreters have differed concerning who is meant by these two adversaries whom God mentioned. Some of them said: one of the two groups is the people of faith, and the other group is the worshippers of idols, from among the polytheists of Quraysh who dueled on the Day of Badr.

Those who said this:

Yaʿqub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Abu Hashim informed us, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear an oath that this verse ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah. He said: ʿAli said: "I am the first, or among the first, who will kneel in dispute before God, blessed and exalted, on the Day of Resurrection."

ʿAli ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muʾammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear by God: "This verse was revealed concerning six men from Quraysh: Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, may God be pleased with them, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ ... to the end of the verse ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ ... to the end of the verse."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear, then he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mahbub narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur ibn al-Mutamir, from Hilal ibn Yasaf, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from some of his companions, from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, who said: "These verses were revealed: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah," up to His words ﴿and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾.

He said: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mujallaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: "By God, this verse was revealed: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ concerning those who went out against one another on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah, may God have mercy on them, Shaybah, ʿUtbah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah."

Others said, among those who said one of the two groups is the faction of faith: "Rather, the other group is the People of the Book."

Those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "They are the People of the Book. They said to the believers: 'We are more entitled to God and earlier in scripture than you, and our prophet came before your prophet.' The believers said: 'We are more entitled to God. We believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and we believed in your prophet and in what God revealed of scripture. You know our scripture and our prophet, then you abandoned them and disbelieved in them out of envy.' That was their dispute concerning their Lord."

Others said: "Rather, the other group is all the disbelievers, of whatever religion they were."

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, from Abu Hamzah, from Jabir, from Mujahid, and ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, and Abu Qazaʿah, from al-Husayn, who said: "They are the disbelievers and the believers, who disputed concerning their Lord."

He narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "Like the disbeliever and the believer." Ibn Jurayj said: "Their dispute concerning which they disputed about their Lord is their dispute in this world, of the people of every religion, who see themselves as more entitled to God than others."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash narrated to us, saying: "ʿAsim and al-Kalbi both used to say concerning ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾: 'The people of polytheism and Islam, when they disputed as to which of them was better.' He said: 'Polytheism made it a religion.'"

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "Like the believer and the disbeliever, their dispute concerning the Resurrection."

Others said: "The two adversaries whom God mentioned in this verse are Paradise and Hell."

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, from Abu Hamzah, from Jabir, from ʿIkrimah, regarding ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "They are Paradise and Hell, who disputed. Hell said: 'God created me for His punishment.' Paradise said: 'God created me for His mercy.' God has related to you of their story what you hear."

The most correct of these opinions in my view, and the most fitting to the interpretation of the verse, is the view of the one who said: "By the two adversaries is meant all the disbelievers of whatever categories of disbelief they were, and all the believers." I only said this is more correct because He, the Exalted, mentioned before this two categories of His creation: one of them, the people who obey Him by prostrating to Him, and the other, the people who disobey Him, upon whom punishment is due. He said: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon﴾, then He said: ﴿and many of mankind, but many deserve the punishment﴾. Then He followed that with a description of both categories and what He will do to them, saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, and God said: ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Thus it was clear by this that what lies between them is news about the two of them.

If someone says: "What do you say about what was related from Abu Dharr, that it was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr?" It is said: "That is, God willing, as it was related from him. But a verse may be revealed due to a cause among the causes, and then be general in everything similar to that cause. This is one of those. The ones who dueled were, one of the two groups, the people of polytheism and disbelief in God, and the other the people of faith in God and obedience to Him. So every disbeliever, in the category of the polytheist group, is an adversary to the people of faith. Likewise, every believer, in the category of the faith group, is an adversary to the people of polytheism."

Thus the meaning of the statement is: "These two adversaries dispute concerning the religion of their Lord, and their dispute in that is each group's enmity toward the other and its fighting against it over its religion."

* *

And His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾

He, the Exalted, says: As for the disbeliever in God among them, garments of fire will be cut out for him, a shirt of brass of fire.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, he said: "The disbeliever has garments of fire cut out for him, while the believer, God admits him into gardens beneath which rivers flow."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yaʿqub narrated to us, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿid, regarding His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, he said: "Garments of brass, and nothing among vessels is hotter or more intense in heat than it."

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "The disbelievers have garments of fire cut out for them, and the believer enters gardens beneath which rivers flow."

* *

And His words: ﴿and boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾

He says: boiling water will be poured over their heads.

As related:

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Taliqani narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Saʿid ibn Zayd, from Abu al-Samh, from Ibn Juhayrah, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, the boiling water is poured upon their heads, and it pierces the skull until it reaches their insides, and it melts what is in their insides until it reaches their feet, and that is the ṣahr (melting). Then they are restored as they were."

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Yaʿmar ibn Bishr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, saying: Saʿid ibn Zayd informed us, from Abu al-Samh, from Ibn Juhayrah, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with the like of it, except that he said: "It pierces the skull until it reaches their insides, and it melts [[yaslat fi jawfih min bab nasara: i.e., it cuts through and uproots it.]] what is in their insides."

Some of them claimed that His words ﴿and for them are hooks of iron﴾ are among the postponed (muʾakhkhar) elements whose meaning is anticipated (muqaddam). They said: The construction of the statement is: "As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire have been cut out for them, and for them are hooks of iron. Boiling water will be poured over their heads." They said: It must be so, because the angel strikes him with an iron hook until it pierces his head, then boiling water whose heat has become intense is poured into it, cutting through his belly. The report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that we mentioned indicates the opposite of what this speaker said, because he (ﷺ) informed that when boiling water is poured over their heads, it pierces the skull until it reaches their insides. This is also what the interpreters' explanation came with. If the hooks had pierced their heads before the boiling water was poured on them, the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "Indeed the boiling water pierces the skull," would have no meaning. Rather, the matter is contrary to what this speaker said.

* *

And His words: ﴿With it, what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted﴾

He says: With the boiling water that is poured over their heads, what is in their bellies of fats is melted, and their skins are roasted by it and fall off. Ṣahr means melting. It is said of it: "I melted the fat with fire" when I melt it, I ṣahr it, ṣahran. From it is the poet's saying:

*You bring water to a stone [lāqī] cast upon a bare plain,
The sun melts it, yet it does not melt.* [[The verse is by Ibn Ahmar describing a sandgrouse chick (Lisan: ṣ-h-r). He said: "The sun ṣahrahu ṣahran" and "ṣahrahu": its heat strikes it intensely and pains its brain, and "inṣahara" is he. Ibn Ahmar describes a sandgrouse chick... the verse; i.e., the sun melts it, so it endures that. "Tarwi" means it brings water to it, as if it were a water-carrier for it; one says: "I gave my family water and they got water": I brought them water. Ṣahr: melting of fat; "ṣahara al-shahm yaṣhuruhu ṣahran": he melted it. In the revelation: "With it, what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted," i.e., melted. "Iṣṭahrahu": he melted it and ate it. "Laqī": everything cast aside and abandoned, like a lost item. "Ṣafṣaf": a smooth, level land, as in Lisan.]]

And from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*He melted the entrails, the roasted, the melted [mustaṣhar]* [[The verse is by al-Ajjaj ibn Ru'bah, the well-known rajaz poet (Lisan: ṣ-h-r). Al-Azhari said: al-ṣahr is melting fat, and al-ṣahārah is what melts of it; likewise al-iṣṭihār is melting, or eating its ṣahārah. Al-Ajjaj said: "He melted the entrails..." The verse is evidence, like the preceding, that ṣahr means melting.]]

And according to what we have said regarding that, the interpreters have spoken.

As related:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿With it will be melted﴾, he said: "It is melted, a melting."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it. Ibn Jurayj said regarding ﴿With it will be melted﴾: "What was cut out for them of punishment."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatadah: ﴿With it, what is in their bellies will be melted﴾, he said: "With it is melted what is in their bellies."

Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 18–22 (part 2 of 2):

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his statement: ﴿Those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ ... up to his statement: ﴿Whereby what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins﴾. He said: They will be given to drink [something] which, when it enters their bellies, melts them, and the skins along with the bellies.

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Ya'qub related to us, from Ja'far and Harun ibn 'Antara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Harun said: "When the people of the Fire become hungry," and Ja'far said: "When the people of the Fire become hungry, they will call for help to the tree of al-Zaqqum, and they will eat from it, and the skins of their faces will be stripped off. So if a passerby were to pass by them, he would recognize them by the skin of their faces in it. Then thirst will overcome them, and they will call for help, and they will be given relief with water like molten brass (al-muhl), which is water whose heat has reached its extreme. When they bring it near their mouths, the flesh of their faces, from which the skins have fallen, will be roasted by its heat. And ﴿whereby what is in their bellies will be melted﴾, meaning their intestines, and their skins will fall off. Then they will be struck with maces of iron, and every limb will fall into its place, and they will call out for destruction and perdition."

* *

As for His statement: ﴿And for them are maces of iron﴾:
The guardians of the Fire will strike their heads with them whenever they try to exit the Fire, until they return them into it.

* *

As for His statement: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it﴾:
He means: whenever these disbelievers, whose attributes Allah has described, wish to exit the Fire because of the distress and anguish that have befallen them, they will be returned to it.

As related by:
⁕ Mujahid ibn Musa related to us, saying: Ja'far ibn 'Awn related to us, saying: al-A'mash informed us, from Abu Zabyan, who said: "The Fire is black and dark; its flame does not give light, nor do its embers." Then he recited: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it﴾. It has been mentioned that they try to escape the Fire when Hell surges and throws those within it up to its highest gates; they wish to get out, but the guardians return them into it with maces, and when they strike them with the maces, they say to them: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾. By His statement ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾ it is meant: it is said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire." It was also said "the punishment of the burning," and the meaning is "the burning [punishment]," just as it is said "the painful punishment," meaning "the painful [punishment]."

**The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many of mankind? But many deserve the punishment.﴾**

He, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ):

Have you not seen, O Muhammad, with your heart, so that you know that God is prostrated to by whoever is in the heavens, from among the angels, and whoever is on the earth, from among creation, from among the jinn and others, and the sun, the moon, and the stars in the sky, and the mountains, and the trees, and the creatures on the earth? The prostration of these is their shadows, when the sun rises upon them and when it declines. Whenever the shadow of anything shifts, that is its prostration.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾, he said: "These are all shadows."

As for the prostration of the sun, the moon and the stars, it is as follows.

As related:

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi ʿAdiyy and Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, the two of them saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu al-ʿAliyah al-Riyahi say: "There is no star in the sky, nor sun, nor moon, but it falls prostrate before God when it sets. Then it does not move until it is permitted, and it takes its course to the right." Muhammad added: "until it returns to its place of rising."

* *

And His words: ﴿and many of mankind﴾

He says: many of the children of Adam prostrate, and they are the believers in God.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿and many of mankind﴾, he said: "The believers."

* *

And His words: ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾

He, the Exalted, says: many of the children of Adam deserve the punishment of God, and it is incumbent upon them because of their disbelief in Him, yet even so their shadows prostrate to God.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾, and "they prostrate along with their shadows." Thus, according to this interpretation that we have mentioned from Mujahid, the words ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿and many of mankind﴾, and it is included among those whom God described as prostrating to Him, and His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾ are a complement of "many." If the second "many" referred to those not included among those described as prostrating, it would be in the nominative case governed by the pronoun referring back to it in His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾, and the meaning of the statement would then be: "and many refused prostration," because His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾ indicate disobedience to God and refusal to prostrate, for which they deserved punishment.

18

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Whomever God humiliates, there is none to honor him. Indeed God does what He wills﴾ (17)

He, the Exalted, says: Whomever God humiliates among His creation, and so makes him wretched, ﴿there is none to honor him﴾ with happiness, by which He makes him happy, because all affairs are in the hand of God. He grants success to whom He wills in obedience to Him, forsakes whom He wills, makes wretched whom He intends, and makes happy whom He loves.

* *

And His words: ﴿Indeed God does what He wills﴾

He, the Exalted, says: Indeed God does what He wills among His creation, humiliating whom He wills to humiliate and honoring whom He wills to honor, because the creation is His creation and the command is His command. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾. It has been reported that some of them recited it as ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ مُكْرَمٍ﴾ (fa-ma lahu min mukramin, with the fatha on the mim of mukram), meaning: "there is none to give him honor." But that is a recitation I do not consider permissible, because of the consensus (ijma') of the authorities among the reciters against it.

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads. With it, what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted. And for them are hooks of iron. Every time they wish to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it, and [they will be told], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ (19–22)

The interpreters have differed concerning who is meant by these two adversaries whom God mentioned. Some of them said: one of the two groups is the people of faith, and the other group is the worshippers of idols, from among the polytheists of Quraysh who dueled on the Day of Badr.

Those who said this:

Yaʿqub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Abu Hashim informed us, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear an oath that this verse ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah. He said: ʿAli said: "I am the first, or among the first, who will kneel in dispute before God, blessed and exalted, on the Day of Resurrection."

ʿAli ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muʾammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear by God: "This verse was revealed concerning six men from Quraysh: Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, may God be pleased with them, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ ... to the end of the verse ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ ... to the end of the verse."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear, then he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mahbub narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur ibn al-Mutamir, from Hilal ibn Yasaf, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from some of his companions, from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, who said: "These verses were revealed: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah," up to His words ﴿and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾.

He said: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mujallaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: "By God, this verse was revealed: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ concerning those who went out against one another on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah, may God have mercy on them, Shaybah, ʿUtbah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah."

Others said, among those who said one of the two groups is the faction of faith: "Rather, the other group is the People of the Book."

Those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "They are the People of the Book. They said to the believers: 'We are more entitled to God and earlier in scripture than you, and our prophet came before your prophet.' The believers said: 'We are more entitled to God. We believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and we believed in your prophet and in what God revealed of scripture. You know our scripture and our prophet, then you abandoned them and disbelieved in them out of envy.' That was their dispute concerning their Lord."

Others said: "Rather, the other group is all the disbelievers, of whatever religion they were."

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, from Abu Hamzah, from Jabir, from Mujahid, and ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, and Abu Qazaʿah, from al-Husayn, who said: "They are the disbelievers and the believers, who disputed concerning their Lord."

He narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "Like the disbeliever and the believer." Ibn Jurayj said: "Their dispute concerning which they disputed about their Lord is their dispute in this world, of the people of every religion, who see themselves as more entitled to God than others."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash narrated to us, saying: "ʿAsim and al-Kalbi both used to say concerning ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾: 'The people of polytheism and Islam, when they disputed as to which of them was better.' He said: 'Polytheism made it a religion.'"

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "Like the believer and the disbeliever, their dispute concerning the Resurrection."

Others said: "The two adversaries whom God mentioned in this verse are Paradise and Hell."

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, from Abu Hamzah, from Jabir, from ʿIkrimah, regarding ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "They are Paradise and Hell, who disputed. Hell said: 'God created me for His punishment.' Paradise said: 'God created me for His mercy.' God has related to you of their story what you hear."

The most correct of these opinions in my view, and the most fitting to the interpretation of the verse, is the view of the one who said: "By the two adversaries is meant all the disbelievers of whatever categories of disbelief they were, and all the believers." I only said this is more correct because He, the Exalted, mentioned before this two categories of His creation: one of them, the people who obey Him by prostrating to Him, and the other, the people who disobey Him, upon whom punishment is due. He said: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon﴾, then He said: ﴿and many of mankind, but many deserve the punishment﴾. Then He followed that with a description of both categories and what He will do to them, saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, and God said: ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Thus it was clear by this that what lies between them is news about the two of them.

If someone says: "What do you say about what was related from Abu Dharr, that it was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr?" It is said: "That is, God willing, as it was related from him. But a verse may be revealed due to a cause among the causes, and then be general in everything similar to that cause. This is one of those. The ones who dueled were, one of the two groups, the people of polytheism and disbelief in God, and the other the people of faith in God and obedience to Him. So every disbeliever, in the category of the polytheist group, is an adversary to the people of faith. Likewise, every believer, in the category of the faith group, is an adversary to the people of polytheism."

Thus the meaning of the statement is: "These two adversaries dispute concerning the religion of their Lord, and their dispute in that is each group's enmity toward the other and its fighting against it over its religion."

* *

And His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾

He, the Exalted, says: As for the disbeliever in God among them, garments of fire will be cut out for him, a shirt of brass of fire.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, he said: "The disbeliever has garments of fire cut out for him, while the believer, God admits him into gardens beneath which rivers flow."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yaʿqub narrated to us, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿid, regarding His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, he said: "Garments of brass, and nothing among vessels is hotter or more intense in heat than it."

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "The disbelievers have garments of fire cut out for them, and the believer enters gardens beneath which rivers flow."

* *

And His words: ﴿and boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾

He says: boiling water will be poured over their heads.

As related:

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Taliqani narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Saʿid ibn Zayd, from Abu al-Samh, from Ibn Juhayrah, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, the boiling water is poured upon their heads, and it pierces the skull until it reaches their insides, and it melts what is in their insides until it reaches their feet, and that is the ṣahr (melting). Then they are restored as they were."

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Yaʿmar ibn Bishr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, saying: Saʿid ibn Zayd informed us, from Abu al-Samh, from Ibn Juhayrah, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with the like of it, except that he said: "It pierces the skull until it reaches their insides, and it melts [[yaslat fi jawfih min bab nasara: i.e., it cuts through and uproots it.]] what is in their insides."

Some of them claimed that His words ﴿and for them are hooks of iron﴾ are among the postponed (muʾakhkhar) elements whose meaning is anticipated (muqaddam). They said: The construction of the statement is: "As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire have been cut out for them, and for them are hooks of iron. Boiling water will be poured over their heads." They said: It must be so, because the angel strikes him with an iron hook until it pierces his head, then boiling water whose heat has become intense is poured into it, cutting through his belly. The report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that we mentioned indicates the opposite of what this speaker said, because he (ﷺ) informed that when boiling water is poured over their heads, it pierces the skull until it reaches their insides. This is also what the interpreters' explanation came with. If the hooks had pierced their heads before the boiling water was poured on them, the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "Indeed the boiling water pierces the skull," would have no meaning. Rather, the matter is contrary to what this speaker said.

* *

And His words: ﴿With it, what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted﴾

He says: With the boiling water that is poured over their heads, what is in their bellies of fats is melted, and their skins are roasted by it and fall off. Ṣahr means melting. It is said of it: "I melted the fat with fire" when I melt it, I ṣahr it, ṣahran. From it is the poet's saying:

*You bring water to a stone [lāqī] cast upon a bare plain,
The sun melts it, yet it does not melt.* [[The verse is by Ibn Ahmar describing a sandgrouse chick (Lisan: ṣ-h-r). He said: "The sun ṣahrahu ṣahran" and "ṣahrahu": its heat strikes it intensely and pains its brain, and "inṣahara" is he. Ibn Ahmar describes a sandgrouse chick... the verse; i.e., the sun melts it, so it endures that. "Tarwi" means it brings water to it, as if it were a water-carrier for it; one says: "I gave my family water and they got water": I brought them water. Ṣahr: melting of fat; "ṣahara al-shahm yaṣhuruhu ṣahran": he melted it. In the revelation: "With it, what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted," i.e., melted. "Iṣṭahrahu": he melted it and ate it. "Laqī": everything cast aside and abandoned, like a lost item. "Ṣafṣaf": a smooth, level land, as in Lisan.]]

And from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*He melted the entrails, the roasted, the melted [mustaṣhar]* [[The verse is by al-Ajjaj ibn Ru'bah, the well-known rajaz poet (Lisan: ṣ-h-r). Al-Azhari said: al-ṣahr is melting fat, and al-ṣahārah is what melts of it; likewise al-iṣṭihār is melting, or eating its ṣahārah. Al-Ajjaj said: "He melted the entrails..." The verse is evidence, like the preceding, that ṣahr means melting.]]

And according to what we have said regarding that, the interpreters have spoken.

As related:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿With it will be melted﴾, he said: "It is melted, a melting."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it. Ibn Jurayj said regarding ﴿With it will be melted﴾: "What was cut out for them of punishment."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatadah: ﴿With it, what is in their bellies will be melted﴾, he said: "With it is melted what is in their bellies."

Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 18–22 (part 2 of 2):

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his statement: ﴿Those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ ... up to his statement: ﴿Whereby what is in their bellies will be melted, and the skins﴾. He said: They will be given to drink [something] which, when it enters their bellies, melts them, and the skins along with the bellies.

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Ya'qub related to us, from Ja'far and Harun ibn 'Antara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Harun said: "When the people of the Fire become hungry," and Ja'far said: "When the people of the Fire become hungry, they will call for help to the tree of al-Zaqqum, and they will eat from it, and the skins of their faces will be stripped off. So if a passerby were to pass by them, he would recognize them by the skin of their faces in it. Then thirst will overcome them, and they will call for help, and they will be given relief with water like molten brass (al-muhl), which is water whose heat has reached its extreme. When they bring it near their mouths, the flesh of their faces, from which the skins have fallen, will be roasted by its heat. And ﴿whereby what is in their bellies will be melted﴾, meaning their intestines, and their skins will fall off. Then they will be struck with maces of iron, and every limb will fall into its place, and they will call out for destruction and perdition."

* *

As for His statement: ﴿And for them are maces of iron﴾:
The guardians of the Fire will strike their heads with them whenever they try to exit the Fire, until they return them into it.

* *

As for His statement: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it﴾:
He means: whenever these disbelievers, whose attributes Allah has described, wish to exit the Fire because of the distress and anguish that have befallen them, they will be returned to it.

As related by:
⁕ Mujahid ibn Musa related to us, saying: Ja'far ibn 'Awn related to us, saying: al-A'mash informed us, from Abu Zabyan, who said: "The Fire is black and dark; its flame does not give light, nor do its embers." Then he recited: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, out of distress, they will be returned into it﴾. It has been mentioned that they try to escape the Fire when Hell surges and throws those within it up to its highest gates; they wish to get out, but the guardians return them into it with maces, and when they strike them with the maces, they say to them: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾. By His statement ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾ it is meant: it is said to them, "Taste the punishment of the Fire." It was also said "the punishment of the burning," and the meaning is "the burning [punishment]," just as it is said "the painful punishment," meaning "the painful [punishment]."

**The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many of mankind? But many deserve the punishment.﴾**

He, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ):

Have you not seen, O Muhammad, with your heart, so that you know that God is prostrated to by whoever is in the heavens, from among the angels, and whoever is on the earth, from among creation, from among the jinn and others, and the sun, the moon, and the stars in the sky, and the mountains, and the trees, and the creatures on the earth? The prostration of these is their shadows, when the sun rises upon them and when it declines. Whenever the shadow of anything shifts, that is its prostration.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾, he said: "These are all shadows."

As for the prostration of the sun, the moon and the stars, it is as follows.

As related:

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi ʿAdiyy and Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, the two of them saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu al-ʿAliyah al-Riyahi say: "There is no star in the sky, nor sun, nor moon, but it falls prostrate before God when it sets. Then it does not move until it is permitted, and it takes its course to the right." Muhammad added: "until it returns to its place of rising."

* *

And His words: ﴿and many of mankind﴾

He says: many of the children of Adam prostrate, and they are the believers in God.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿and many of mankind﴾, he said: "The believers."

* *

And His words: ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾

He, the Exalted, says: many of the children of Adam deserve the punishment of God, and it is incumbent upon them because of their disbelief in Him, yet even so their shadows prostrate to God.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾, and "they prostrate along with their shadows." Thus, according to this interpretation that we have mentioned from Mujahid, the words ﴿but many deserve the punishment﴾ are coordinated with His words ﴿and many of mankind﴾, and it is included among those whom God described as prostrating to Him, and His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾ are a complement of "many." If the second "many" referred to those not included among those described as prostrating, it would be in the nominative case governed by the pronoun referring back to it in His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾, and the meaning of the statement would then be: "and many refused prostration," because His words ﴿deserve the punishment﴾ indicate disobedience to God and refusal to prostrate, for which they deserved punishment.

18

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Whomever God humiliates, there is none to honor him. Indeed God does what He wills﴾ (17)

He, the Exalted, says: Whomever God humiliates among His creation, and so makes him wretched, ﴿there is none to honor him﴾ with happiness, by which He makes him happy, because all affairs are in the hand of God. He grants success to whom He wills in obedience to Him, forsakes whom He wills, makes wretched whom He intends, and makes happy whom He loves.

* *

And His words: ﴿Indeed God does what He wills﴾

He, the Exalted, says: Indeed God does what He wills among His creation, humiliating whom He wills to humiliate and honoring whom He wills to honor, because the creation is His creation and the command is His command. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾. It has been reported that some of them recited it as ﴿فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ مُكْرَمٍ﴾ (fa-ma lahu min mukramin, with the fatha on the mim of mukram), meaning: "there is none to give him honor." But that is a recitation I do not consider permissible, because of the consensus (ijma') of the authorities among the reciters against it.

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads. With it, what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted. And for them are hooks of iron. Every time they wish to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it, and [they will be told], "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ (19–22)

The interpreters have differed concerning who is meant by these two adversaries whom God mentioned. Some of them said: one of the two groups is the people of faith, and the other group is the worshippers of idols, from among the polytheists of Quraysh who dueled on the Day of Badr.

Those who said this:

Yaʿqub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Abu Hashim informed us, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear an oath that this verse ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah. He said: ʿAli said: "I am the first, or among the first, who will kneel in dispute before God, blessed and exalted, on the Day of Resurrection."

ʿAli ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muʾammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear by God: "This verse was revealed concerning six men from Quraysh: Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, may God be pleased with them, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ ... to the end of the verse ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ ... to the end of the verse."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mijlaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: I heard Abu Dharr swear, then he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mahbub narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur ibn al-Mutamir, from Hilal ibn Yasaf, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from some of his companions, from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, who said: "These verses were revealed: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah," up to His words ﴿and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾.

He said: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Abu Hashim, from Abu Mujallaz, from Qays ibn ʿUbad, who said: "By God, this verse was revealed: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ concerning those who went out against one another on the Day of Badr: Hamzah, ʿAli, ʿUbaydah, may God have mercy on them, Shaybah, ʿUtbah, and al-Walid ibn ʿUtbah."

Others said, among those who said one of the two groups is the faction of faith: "Rather, the other group is the People of the Book."

Those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "They are the People of the Book. They said to the believers: 'We are more entitled to God and earlier in scripture than you, and our prophet came before your prophet.' The believers said: 'We are more entitled to God. We believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and we believed in your prophet and in what God revealed of scripture. You know our scripture and our prophet, then you abandoned them and disbelieved in them out of envy.' That was their dispute concerning their Lord."

Others said: "Rather, the other group is all the disbelievers, of whatever religion they were."

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, from Abu Hamzah, from Jabir, from Mujahid, and ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, and Abu Qazaʿah, from al-Husayn, who said: "They are the disbelievers and the believers, who disputed concerning their Lord."

He narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "Like the disbeliever and the believer." Ibn Jurayj said: "Their dispute concerning which they disputed about their Lord is their dispute in this world, of the people of every religion, who see themselves as more entitled to God than others."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash narrated to us, saying: "ʿAsim and al-Kalbi both used to say concerning ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾: 'The people of polytheism and Islam, when they disputed as to which of them was better.' He said: 'Polytheism made it a religion.'"

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "Like the believer and the disbeliever, their dispute concerning the Resurrection."

Others said: "The two adversaries whom God mentioned in this verse are Paradise and Hell."

Those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, from Abu Hamzah, from Jabir, from ʿIkrimah, regarding ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾, he said: "They are Paradise and Hell, who disputed. Hell said: 'God created me for His punishment.' Paradise said: 'God created me for His mercy.' God has related to you of their story what you hear."

The most correct of these opinions in my view, and the most fitting to the interpretation of the verse, is the view of the one who said: "By the two adversaries is meant all the disbelievers of whatever categories of disbelief they were, and all the believers." I only said this is more correct because He, the Exalted, mentioned before this two categories of His creation: one of them, the people who obey Him by prostrating to Him, and the other, the people who disobey Him, upon whom punishment is due. He said: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon﴾, then He said: ﴿and many of mankind, but many deserve the punishment﴾. Then He followed that with a description of both categories and what He will do to them, saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, and God said: ﴿Indeed, God admits those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Thus it was clear by this that what lies between them is news about the two of them.

If someone says: "What do you say about what was related from Abu Dharr, that it was revealed concerning those who dueled on the Day of Badr?" It is said: "That is, God willing, as it was related from him. But a verse may be revealed due to a cause among the causes, and then be general in everything similar to that cause. This is one of those. The ones who dueled were, one of the two groups, the people of polytheism and disbelief in God, and the other the people of faith in God and obedience to Him. So every disbeliever, in the category of the polytheist group, is an adversary to the people of faith. Likewise, every believer, in the category of the faith group, is an adversary to the people of polytheism."

Thus the meaning of the statement is: "These two adversaries dispute concerning the religion of their Lord, and their dispute in that is each group's enmity toward the other and its fighting against it over its religion."

* *

And His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾

He, the Exalted, says: As for the disbeliever in God among them, garments of fire will be cut out for him, a shirt of brass of fire.

As related:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, he said: "The disbeliever has garments of fire cut out for him, while the believer, God admits him into gardens beneath which rivers flow."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yaʿqub narrated to us, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿid, regarding His words: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, he said: "Garments of brass, and nothing among vessels is hotter or more intense in heat than it."
