So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up. Then when they fall on their sides, eat from them and feed the contented and the beggar. Thus We have subjected them to you that you may be grateful﴾

Allah, may He be remembered, says: "Wa-l-budn" is the plural of badanah, and it may be said of its singular: badan. When it is said badan, it may be both a plural and a singular. That it may be said of the singular is shown by the verse of the rajaz poet:

"Upon me, when I possess affairs, is a fast of months that became obligatory as vows,
and a shaved head, full and plaited, and a camel, armored and abundant."

[This is four lines of the rajaz meter, which the author related from al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an at this place of the tafsir, and he had earlier recited three of them at (7:120), at the explanation of His saying: (Then two others from among those who have a claim should stand in their place) in Surat al-Ma'idah, with some variation in wording from his narration here. The words are: "Upon me, when you possess the affairs..." and "...a camel, adorned and slaughtered." The word "badanan" in that narration may be correct, meaning a large, fat camel, as in Lisan al-Arab (b-d-n): a man is "badin," a woman "badin" or "badinah," and the plural is "badan" (with damma and sukun) and "badan" (with damma and a doubled dal). It may also be that "badanan" is a corruption of "badan" (with fatha), by the evidence of the author's rendering of it with his words "wa-l-budn" (with damma and sukun) as the plural of "badanah" (with fatha), and it is said of its singular "badan" (with fatha), which is shown by the poet's verse "wa-badanan mudarra'an mawfuran." End.
This is also supported by the words of Abu al-Baqa' al-'Ukbari in I'rab al-Qur'an: "al-budn" (with damma and sukun) is the plural of "badan" (with fatha), its singular being "badanah," like khashab (with damma and sukun) and khashab (with fatha). It is said to be the plural of "badanah," like thamarah and thamar (the latter with damma and sukun), and it is read with a damma on the dal. The "badanah," as in Lisan al-Arab (b-d-n), takes the ta' marbutah because of its size and fatness. End. The poet says: I obligated upon myself, when I possess the affairs, using the second person, that I fast months, shave my head, and slaughter a camel, meaning a huge camel.]

"Al-badan" is the large of everything, and for this reason Imru' al-Qays ibn al-Nu'man, the lord of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadir, was called "al-badan," because of his bulk and the slackness of his flesh; it is said: "qad badna tabdeenan" (he has grown stout). So the meaning of the statement: and the camels, large of body and bulky, We have made them for you, O people, as among the symbols of Allah — that is, among the signs of the command of Allah which He has commanded you in the rites of your pilgrimage, when you garland them, adorn them with the marks of sacrifice, and mark them, so that it is known and recognized that you have done this with the camels and cattle.

As related by:
- Ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Yahya related to us, from Ibn Juraij, who said: 'Ata' said: ﴿And the camels — We have made them for you as among the symbols of Allah﴾: the cow and the camel.

* *

And His saying: ﴿For you therein is good﴾

That is: for you in the camels there is good. That good is reward in the Hereafter through slaughtering them and giving them in charity, and in this world: riding them when you are in need of riding them.

The people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said.

Among those who said that:
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, and al-Harith told me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of Allah: ﴿For you therein is good﴾: "Reward and benefits in the camels."
- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.
- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿For you therein is good﴾: "Milk and riding when one is in need."
- 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan related to us, saying: Ishaq informed us, from Sharik, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿For you therein is good﴾: "When you are compelled to your camel, ride it and drink its milk."
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿For you therein is good﴾: "Whoever needs the back of the camel rides it, and whoever needs its milk drinks it."

* *

And His saying: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾

That is, He, may He be remembered, says: So mention the name of Allah over the camels at the time of slaughtering them, while they are lined up (ṣawāff).

The readers differed in the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of the regional centres recited ﴿ṣawāffa⁠﴾ (ṣawāff) meaning "lined up," its singular being ṣāffah, and it is said: "ṣaffat bayna yadayhā" (she was lined up before her). It is narrated from al-Hasan, Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam, and a group of others with them that they recited it "ṣawāfiya" with a ya', in the accusative, meaning: sincerely for Allah, having no partner in them, purely for Him.

And some of them recited it "ṣawāff," dropping the ya' and nunating the letter, after the pattern of 'iwar and 'awad. And it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited it "ṣawāfinn," meaning: tied up (mu'aqqalah).

The correct recitation in my view is the recitation of the one who recited it with a doubled fa' and in the accusative, because of the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it, with the meaning we have mentioned for the one who recited it thus.

Among those who interpreted it according to the reading with a doubled fa' and in the accusative:
- Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Jabir ibn Nuh related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾: He said: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, O Allah, from You and to You." "Ṣawāff": standing on three legs. It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: What do we do with their hides? He said: Give them in charity and benefit from them.
- Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam told me, saying: Ayyub ibn Suwayd related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: "ṣawāff": he said: standing. He said: "Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, O Allah, from You and to You."
- Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi related to us, from Shu'bah, from Sulayman, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾: "Standing on three tied legs, in the name of Allah. Allahu akbar, O Allah, from You and to You."
- Ya'qub told me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Husayn informed us, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿ṣawāff﴾: "Tied at one of its forelegs, standing on three legs."
- 'Ali told me, saying: 'Abd Allah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah told me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾: "Standing."
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, his saying: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾: "Ṣawāff": that one leg is tied and it is stood upon three, and it is slaughtered thus.
- Ya'qub related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Yu'la ibn 'Ata' informed us, saying: Bujayr ibn Salim informed us, saying: I saw Ibn 'Umar slaughtering his camel, and he said: "ṣawāff," as Allah said, and he slaughtered it while it was standing, tied at one of its forelegs.
- Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, saying: Layth informed us, from Mujahid, who said: "Al-ṣawāff": when its leg is tied and it stands on three.
- Layth related to us, from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾: "Lined up between its ankles."
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to us, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith told me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿ṣawāff﴾: "Standing in lines, on three legs."
- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾: "Standing between its hooves."
- Ibn al-Barqi related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Maryam related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub informed us, from Khalid ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Hilal, from Nafi', from 'Abd Allah: that he used to slaughter the camels while they were standing, facing the House, their forelegs lined up with the tethers. He said: These are what Allah mentioned: ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾.
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir told me, from Mansur, from a man, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: I said to him: the saying of Allah ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them while they are lined up﴾. He said: "When you want to slaughter the camel, slaughter it and say: Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, O Allah, from You and to You. Then name it and slaughter it." I said: Shall I say that for the sacrifice? He said: "And for the sacrifice."

Among those who interpreted it according to the reading "ṣawāfiya" with the ya':
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir related to us, from his father, from al-Hasan, that he said: "So mention the name of Allah over them, ṣawāfiya": he said: "Sincerely."
- He said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, who said: al-Hasan said: "ṣawāfiya": "Purely for Allah."
- al-Hasan related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, who said: al-Hasan said: "ṣawāfiya": "purely for Allah."
- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Shaqiq al-Dabbi: "So mention the name of Allah over them, ṣawāfiya": he said: "Pure."
- He said: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Ayman ibn Nabil related to us, who said: I asked Tawus about His saying: "So mention the name of Allah over them, ṣawāfiya": he said: "Pure."
- Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying: "So mention the name of Allah over them, ṣawāfiya": "Pure, without any partner, as the polytheists used to do, making for Allah and for their gods ṣawāfi, pure for Allah, the Exalted."

Among those who interpreted it according to the reading "ṣawāfina":
- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "So mention the name of Allah over them, ṣawāfin": that is, tied, standing.
- al-Hasan related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "So mention the name of Allah over them, ṣawāfin": that is, tied, standing.
- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: "Whoever recites it ṣawāfin says: tied. And whoever recites it ﴿ṣawāff⁠﴾ says: it lines up its feet between its forelegs."
- I was told, from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His saying: "So mention the name of Allah over them, ṣawāff": meaning ṣawāfin, and the camel, when slaughtered, has one foreleg tied, so it stands on three, and thus it is slaughtered.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The explanation of the most correct of these sayings concerning His saying ﴿ṣawāff﴾ has already preceded: they are those lined up before their owners, with one of their legs tied.

* *

And His saying: ﴿So when they fall on their sides﴾

That is: when they fall and their sides come down to the ground after slaughter. ﴿Then eat from them﴾ — and it is from the expression: "wajabat al-shams" when the sun has set and falls for its setting. And from it is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"Has the sun not been eclipsed, and the full moon, and the stars, for the fallen mountain?" [This is the verse of Aws ibn Hajar as the author said. "The mountain" here: he means by it a great man, and "al-wajib" is the one who died. It is said in Lisan al-Arab (w-j-b): "wajab al-rajul wajaban": he died. Qays ibn al-Khatim said describing a war which occurred between the Aws and the Khazraj on the day of Bu'ath, when the leader of Banu 'Awf and their commander persisted in fighting and forbade Banu 'Awf from peace until the first slain fell:
"Banu 'Awf obeyed a commander who forbade them peace, until the first fallen one."
And the verse of Aws ibn Hajar is evidence that His saying, the Exalted: "fa-idha wajabat junubuha" means: when they fall and their sides come down to the ground after slaughter, then eat from them. End.]. He means by "al-wajib": the fallen.

The people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said.

Among those who said that:
- Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith told me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿So when they fall on their sides﴾: "They fall to the ground."
- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.
- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, concerning His saying: ﴿So when they fall on their sides﴾: "When it has finished and been slaughtered."
- Muhammad ibn 'Ammarah related to us, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa related to us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Abu Yahya, from Mujahid: ﴿So when they fall﴾: "Slaughtered."
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, his saying: ﴿So when they fall on their sides﴾: "When it is slaughtered."
- Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying: ﴿So when they fall on their sides﴾: "When they die."

* *

And His saying: ﴿So eat from them﴾

This is in the form of a command, but its meaning is permission and allowance. Allah says: When it is slaughtered and falls dead after slaughter, then its eating has become lawful for you, and it is not a command of obligation.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i used to say concerning this, as related to us: Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, both saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, who said: The polytheists would not eat from their slaughtered animals, so it was permitted for the Muslims, and they ate from them. Whoever wills eats, and whoever wills does not eat.

- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Mu'ammal related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Husayn, from Mujahid, who said: If he wills he eats, and if he wills he does not eat. It is in the position of: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾.
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿So eat from them and feed the contented and the beggar﴾: he says: he eats from it and feeds.
- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Yunus informed us, from al-Hasan; Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim; Hajjaj informed us, from 'Ata'; and Husayn informed us, from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿So eat from them﴾: "If he wills he eats, and if he wills he does not eat." Mujahid said: It is a concession, like His saying: ﴿Then when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land﴾, and like His saying: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾, and His saying: ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾, meaning: feed from it the contented.

The people of interpretation differed concerning who is meant by "al-qani'" (the contented) and "al-mu'tarr" (the beggar). Some of them said: "al-qani'" is the one who is content with what is given to him or with what he has and does not ask, and "al-mu'tarr" is the one who presents himself to you so that you feed him from the meat without his asking.

Among those who said that:
- Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And feed the contented and the beggar﴾: he said: "The contented: the one who is self-sufficient with what you have given him while he is in his house, and the beggar: the one who presents himself to you and approaches you that you feed him from the meat without asking. These are the ones he was commanded to feed from the camels."
- Ya'qub told me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: "The contented: your neighbour who is content with what you have given him, and the beggar: the one who presents himself to you and does not ask you."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 22, verses 35–36 (part 2 of 2):

⁕ Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Abu Sakhr informed me, on the authority of al-Qurazi, that he used to say about this verse: ﴿And feed the contented and the beggar﴾. "The contented (al-qani') is the one who is content with a little thing and is satisfied with it. The beggar (al-mu'tarr) is the one who passes by your side and does not ask anything; that is the beggar."

And others said: "The contented is the one who is content with what he has and does not ask. The beggar is the one who approaches you and asks you."

Mention of those who said that: Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiya told me, on the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talha, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿the contented and the beggar﴾: "He means the contented is the one who abstains (al-mutacaffif), and the beggar is the one who asks."

⁕ Ibn Abi al-Shawarib related to us, saying: Abd al-Wahid told us, saying: Khusayf told us, saying: I heard Mujahid say: "The contented: the people of Makkah. The beggar: the one who approaches you and asks you."

⁕ Abu al-Sa'ib related to me, saying: Ata told us, on the authority of Khusayf, on the authority of Mujahid, the same.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim told us, saying: Ka'b ibn Farukh told me, saying: I heard Qatada narrate, on the authority of Ikrima, regarding His saying ﴿the contented and the beggar﴾: "The contented: the one who sits in his house. The beggar: the one who asks."

⁕ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-A'la told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatada, who said: "The contented: the abstaining one who sits in his house. The beggar: the one who approaches you and asks you."

⁕ Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr told us, on the authority of Ma'mar, on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: "The contented and the beggar. [He said:] The contented: the one who covets what is with you but does not ask you. The beggar: the one who approaches you and asks you."

⁕ Nasr ibn Abd al-Rahman related to me, saying: al-Muharibi told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid and Ibrahim, who both said: "The contented: the one who sits in his house. The beggar: the one who asks you."

⁕ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-A'la told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding the contented and the beggar, who said: "The contented: the one who is content with what is in his hands. The beggar: the one who approaches you. And both of them have a right upon you, O son of Adam."

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding ﴿So eat from them and feed the contented and the beggar﴾: "The contented: the one who sits in his house. The beggar: the one who approaches you."

And others said: "The contented: he is the one who asks, and the beggar: he is the one who approaches you without asking."

Mention of those who said that: Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-A'la told us, saying: Yunus told us, on the authority of al-Hasan, who said: "The contented: the one who comes to you in supplication and asks you. The beggar: the one who presents himself to you and does not ask you."

⁕ Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'ba told us, on the authority of Mansur ibn Zadhan, on the authority of al-Hasan, regarding this verse ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾, who said: "The contented: the one who is content. The beggar: the one who approaches you." He said: "And al-Kalbi said: The contented: the one who asks you; and the beggar: the one who approaches you, presenting himself and not asking you."

⁕ Nasr Abd al-Rahman al-Awdi related to me, saying: al-Muharibi told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Yunus, on the authority of al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾, who said: "The contented: the one who asks you. The beggar: the one who presents himself to you."

⁕ Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris told us, on the authority of his father, who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The contented: the one who asks."

⁕ Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Ahmasi related to me, saying: Ghalib told me, saying: Shurayk told me, on the authority of Furat al-Qazzaz, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying ﴿the contented﴾, who said: "He is the one who asks." Then he said: "Have you not heard the verse of al-Shammakh:

"The wealth of a man, when it sets him right, makes him rich
and keeps him from poverty, is more chaste than begging."

[[The line is by al-Shammakh ibn Dirar (Lisan al-Arab: q-n-'). He said: In the revelation: ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾; so the contented is the one who asks, and the beggar is the one who presents himself without asking. Al-Shammakh said: "The wealth of a man..." meaning from asking people. Ibn al-Sikkit said: Some Arabs permit al-qunu' in the sense of qana'a (contentment), but the good Arabic usage is the first. It is also transmitted as "min al-kunu'," and al-kunu' means contraction and humbling oneself. It was also said: al-qani' is the asker; it was said: the abstainer; and each is suitable. The man is qani' and qanii'. Al-Farra' said: he is the one who asks you, and you give him before he asks. It was also said: al-qunu' is covetousness. The verb: qana, with a fatha, yaqna'u qunu'an, meaning he humbled himself in asking; it was also said: he asked. Mafaqira: the aspects of his poverty; it was said it is the plural of faqr on an irregular pattern, like al-mushabih and al-malamih. It may also be the plural of mufaqqira, the verbal noun of afqarahu, or the plural of mufaqqar (active participle).]]

He said: "From asking."

⁕ Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn Ulayya told us, saying: Yunus informed us, on the authority of al-Hasan, that he said regarding His saying ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾: "The contented: the one who comes to you in supplication and asks you. The beggar: the one who shows you his condition and presents himself to you without asking."

⁕ al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hisham told us, saying: Mansur and Yunus informed us, on the authority of al-Hasan, who said: "The contented: the asker. The beggar: the one who presents himself and does not ask."

⁕ Yunus related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Ayyash informed me, saying: Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The contented: the one who asks people."

And others said: "The contented: the neighbour; the beggar: the one who approaches you from among the people."

Mention of those who said that: Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris told us, saying: I heard Layth, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: "The contented: your neighbour, even if he is rich. The beggar: the one who approaches you."

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam told us, on the authority of Anbasa, on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, who said: Mujahid said, regarding His saying ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾: "The contented: your wealthy neighbour. The beggar: whoever approaches you from among the people."

⁕ Ya'qub related to me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Mughira informed us, on the authority of Ibrahim, regarding His saying ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾, that he said: "One of them is the asker, and the other is the neighbour."

And others said: "The contented: the wanderer (al-tawwaf); the beggar: the visiting friend."

Mention of those who said that: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam related to me, saying: My father and Shu'ayb ibn al-Layth told me, on the authority of al-Layth, on the authority of Khalid ibn Yazid, on the authority of Ibn Abi Hilal, who said: Zayd ibn Aslam said, regarding the words of God Almighty ﴿the contented and the beggar﴾: "The contented: the poor man who goes around (from door to door). The beggar: the friend and the weak person who visits."

And others said: "The contented: the covetous; the beggar: the one who comes to you with his body (in need of the meat)."

Mention of those who said that: Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us, all on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿the contented﴾: "The covetous. And the beggar: the one who comes to you with his body, whether rich or poor."

⁕ al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Umar ibn Ata informed me, on the authority of Ikrima, who said: "The contented: the covetous."

And others said: "The contented: he is the destitute, and the beggar: the one who comes to the meat."

Mention of those who said that: Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿and feed the contented and the beggar﴾: "The contented: the destitute. The beggar: the one who comes to a people for their meat, and he is not destitute, and he has no sacrificial animal; he comes to the people for the sake of their meat. And the wretched poor man: he is the contented."

And others said, with what Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Furat, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The contented: the one who is content. The beggar: the one who approaches you."

⁕ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Yunus, on the authority of al-Hasan, the same.

⁕ He said: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Mansur, on the authority of Ibrahim and Mujahid, regarding ﴿the contented and the beggar﴾: "The contented: the one who sits in his house. The beggar: the one who presents himself to you."

The most correct of these opinions is the view of the one who said: what is meant by the contented is the asker. For if what was meant by "the contented" in this place were the one who is satisfied with what he has and is self-sufficient, it would have been said: "and feed the contented and the asker," not "and feed the contented and the beggar." Following it with His words "and the beggar" is clear proof that the contented means the asker, from the expression qana'a fulan ila fulan, meaning he asked him and humbled himself before him; he qan'a qunu'an. From this is the verse of Labid:

"The master gave me when I was in poverty,
when he said: 'Look at my need and my humbling (qunu'i).'"

[[The line is by Labid, as the author said; I did not find it in his diwan in the Leiden edition of 1891. Al-khulla with a fatha means need and poverty. Al-Lihyani said: khulla bihi shadida, meaning destitution. Al-qunu' means asking; we have explained it in the preceding witness.]]

As for the contented in the sense of the self-sufficient, it comes from qanit (with the nun vowelled with a kasra), aqna'u, qana'atan, qan'an, and qan'anan. As for the beggar (al-mu'tarr), he is the one who comes to you presenting himself as needy of you, so that you give him and feed him.

* *

As for His saying ﴿Thus We have subjected them to you﴾: it means: "Thus We have subjected the camels to you, O people, so that you may give thanks to Me for subjecting them to you."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 37–38:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿It is not their meat, nor their blood, that reaches God, but it is your piety that reaches Him. Thus He has subjected them to you that you may magnify God for guiding you. And give good tidings to the good-doers.﴾ (37)

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The meat of your sacrificial animals and their blood do not reach God, but your piety toward Him reaches Him, when you fear Him regarding them, intend thereby His countenance, act concerning them in accordance with what He has recommended and commanded you regarding their matter, and magnify His sacred things through them.

Ahl al-ta'wil (the scholars of interpretation) have said the same as what we have said concerning that.

Mention of those who said that:
Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, regarding the saying of God: ﴿It is not their meat, nor their blood, that reaches God, but it is your piety that reaches Him﴾, he said: "What is intended thereby is the countenance of God."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿It is not their meat, nor their blood, that reaches God, but it is your piety that reaches Him﴾, he said: "If you fear God regarding these camels, and act regarding them for God, and seek what God mentioned by way of magnifying the rites of God and the sacred things of God, then, for He said: ﴿And whoever magnifies the rites of God, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾, and He said: ﴿And whoever magnifies the sacred things of God, it is better for him with his Lord﴾." He said: "And [you] made it good, and that is what God accepts. As for the meat and the blood, how could they reach God?"

His saying: ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾ means: Thus He has subjected the camels to you. He says: ﴿that you may magnify God for guiding you﴾, meaning: that you may exalt God for what He has guided you to, namely His granting you success in His religion and in the rites of your pilgrimage.

As also: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿that you may magnify God for guiding you﴾, he said: "For slaughtering them on those days."

﴿And give good tidings to the good-doers﴾: He says: And give good tidings, O Muhammad, to those who obeyed God and did good in their obedience to Him in this world, with Paradise in the Hereafter.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, God defends those who believe. Indeed, God does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾ (38)

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed God repels the harm of the polytheists from those who believe in God and His Messenger. Indeed God does not love every treacherous one who betrays God by opposing His command and prohibition, disobeys Him, and obeys Satan. ﴿Ungrateful﴾ means: one who denies His blessings upon him, not recognizing the right of the Giver of them to be thanked for them. It was also said that this refers to God's repelling the disbelievers of Quraysh from those among the believers who were amongst them before their migration.

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed God repels the harm of the polytheists from those who believe in God and His Messenger. Indeed God does not love every treacherous one who betrays God by opposing His command and prohibition, disobeys Him, and obeys Satan. ﴿Ungrateful﴾ means: one who denies His blessings upon him, not recognizing the right of the Giver of them to be thanked for them. **On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. And indeed, Allah is capable of helping them.﴾ (22:39)**

Its meaning: God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Allah gave permission to the believers who fight the polytheists in His cause, because the polytheists had wronged them by fighting them.

The reciters differed over how this is recited. The majority of the reciters of Medina read ﴿أُذِنَ﴾ with a ḍamma on the alif, and ﴿يُقاتَلُونَ﴾ with a fatḥa on the tā', so that both ʾudhina and yuqātalūna are in the passive form, with the agent unnamed. Some of the Kufans and the majority of the reciters of Basra read ʾudhina in the passive, and "yuqātilūna" with a kasra on the tā', meaning: those who have been given permission to fight fight the polytheists. The majority of the Kufan reciters and some of the Meccan reciters read "ʾadhina" with a fatḥa on the alif, meaning: Allah gave permission, and "yuqātilūna" with a kasra on the tā', meaning: those to whom Allah gave permission to fight are fighting the polytheists. These three readings (qirāʾāt, the recognised modes of recitation) are close in meaning. Those who read ʾudhina in the passive, the meaning in interpretation returns to the meaning of the reading of one who reads it in the active with the agent named. As for one who reads yuqātilūna, and yuqātalūna with kasra or fatḥa, the meaning of one of them is close to the meaning of the other, because whoever fights a person, the one he fights is a fighter too, and each of them is a fighter. Since that is so, whichever of these readings the reciter uses, he is correct.

However, the reading most beloved to me is ʾadhina with a fatḥa on the alif, meaning: Allah gave permission, because this is closer to His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate﴾. Allah gave permission regarding those He does not love, to those who fight them, by their fighting. So ʾadhina refers back to His words ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love﴾. Likewise, the reading most beloved to me for yuqātilūna is with a kasra on the tā', meaning: those who fight those whom Allah has informed us He does not love, so that the speech is connected in meaning, each part to the next.

Scholars differed about who is meant by the permission to fight in this verse. Some said it refers to the Prophet of Allah and his companions.

Those who said this include: Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. And indeed, Allah is capable of helping them﴾: it means Muḥammad and his companions when they were driven out of Mecca to Medina. God says: ﴿And indeed, Allah is capable of helping them﴾, and He did so.

Ibn Bashshār related to us, saying: Abū Aḥmad related to us, saying: Sufyān related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Muslim al-Baṭīn, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) left Mecca, a man said: "They have driven out their Prophet!" So the verse was revealed: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾ … ﴿those who have been driven from their homes without right﴾, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions.

Yaḥyā ibn Dāwūd al-Wāsiṭī related to us, saying: Isḥāq ibn Yūsuf related to us, from Sufyān, from al-Aʿmash, from Muslim, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) left Mecca, Abū Bakr said: "They have driven out their Prophet! Surely to God we belong and to Him we return! They will surely perish!" Ibn ʿAbbās said: So Allah revealed: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged, and indeed, Allah is capable of helping them﴾. Abū Bakr said: "Then I knew that there would be fighting." And this was the first verse revealed. Ibn Dāwūd said: Ibn Isḥāq said: They used to read ﴿ʾUdhina﴾ (in the passive), and we read "ʾAdhina" (in the active).

Ibn Wakīʿ related to us, saying: Isḥāq related to us, from Sufyān, from al-Aʿmash, from Muslim, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) left… and then he mentioned something similar, except that he said: Abū Bakr said: "I knew that there would be fighting." Up to this point his narration ended, and he added nothing to it.

Muḥammad ibn Khalaf al-ʿAsqalānī related to me, saying: Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf related to us, saying: Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ related to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Muslim, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left Mecca, Abū Bakr said: "Surely to God we belong and to Him we return! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has been driven out! By God, they will all surely perish!" When the verse was revealed: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾ up to His words: ﴿those who have been driven from their homes without right﴾, Abū Bakr knew that there would be fighting.

Yūnus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾: He gave them permission to fight them after He had pardoned them for ten years. He recited: ﴿those who have been driven from their homes without right﴾, and said: "These are the believers."

I was told on the authority of al-Ḥusayn, who said: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say, regarding His words: ﴿those who have been driven from their homes without right﴾. [[Perhaps he abbreviated it, unless something fell out from the copyist's text; the original would be: "they and the Prophet and his companions," or something similar.]]

Others said: Rather, this verse refers to specific people who had left the abode of war wishing to emigrate, and were prevented from doing so.

Those who said this include: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us (and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqāʾ related to us, all together), from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding the words of Allah: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾: He said: They were believing people who left Mecca as emigrants to Medina, and they were being prevented, so Allah gave permission to the believers to fight the disbelievers, and they fought them.

al-Qāsim related to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn related to us, saying: Ḥajjāj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, regarding His words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾: He said: Some believers left Mecca as emigrants to Medina, and they were being prevented, so the disbelievers overtook them, and Allah gave permission to the believers to fight the disbelievers, and they fought them. Ibn Jurayj said: He means: the first fighting that Allah permitted for the believers.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: "ʾUdhina lil-ladhīna yuqātalūna fī sabīl Allāh" (Permission is given to those who are fought in the cause of Allah). Qatādah said: And it is the first verse revealed about fighting, so He gave them permission to fight.

al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾: He said: It is the first verse revealed about fighting, so He gave them permission to fight. Some of them claimed that Allah only said: "Permission is given to those who fight," with the fighting, because the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to kill the disbelievers secretly, when they harmed them and were severe against them in Mecca before the Hijrah. So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate﴾. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions emigrated to Medina, He permitted them to kill and fight them, and He said: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾. This is a view reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim by a route that is not firmly established.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And indeed, Allah is capable of helping them﴾.

Its meaning: May His majesty be praised: And indeed, Allah is capable of giving victory to the believers who fight in the cause of Allah, and He has indeed helped them, honoured and exalted them, destroyed their enemy, and humbled them at their hands.

The Exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah." And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, there would have been demolished monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned. And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.﴾ (22:40)

His words, may His remembrance be exalted: Permission is given to those who are fighting, ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾. The second "alladhina" (those who) refers back to the first "alladhina." By "those expelled from their homes" He means the believers whom the disbelievers of Quraysh expelled from Makkah. Their expulsion from their homes, the torture of some of them for their faith in Allah and His Messenger, the reviling of some of them with their tongues, and the threats against them, until they were compelled to leave, were all carried out by them. Their conduct toward them was without right, because the disbelievers were upon falsehood while the believers were upon the truth. Therefore He, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾.

* *

His words: ﴿only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah."﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: They were not expelled from their homes except because they said, "Our Lord is Allah alone, with no partner." The "an" (that) is in the genitive position as a substitution for the "bi" (by/with) in His words ﴿without right﴾. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative position as an exception.

* *

His words: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of this. Some of them said: the meaning is: and were it not for Allah's repelling the polytheists by means of the Muslims.

Mention of who said that: Al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His words: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾, "the repelling of the polytheists by means of the Muslims."

Others said: the meaning is: and were it not for fighting and jihad in the way of Allah.

Mention of who said that: Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾, "Were it not for fighting and jihad."

Others said: rather, the meaning is: and were it not for Allah's repelling by means of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) those who came after them from the Successors.

Mention of who said that: Ibrahim ibn Sa'id related to us, he said: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to us, from Sayf ibn 'Amr, from Abu Ruq, from Thabit ibn 'Awsaja al-Hadrami, who said: twenty-seven men from the companions of 'Ali and 'Abd Allah related to me, among them Lahiq ibn al-Aqmar, al-'Ayzar ibn Jarwal, and 'Atiyya al-Qurazi, that 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: This verse was revealed only concerning the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾, "were it not for Allah's defense by means of the Companions of Muhammad against the Successors" ﴿there would have been demolished monasteries and churches﴾.

Others said: rather, the meaning is: were it not that Allah repels by means of those whose testimony is accepted in rights, so that there are rights between some people and others, from those whose testimony is not permissible and others; thereby He preserves this one's wealth and by this means protects this one's blood from being shed, and they abandon injustices on his account, lest people wrong one another; then monasteries would be destroyed.

Mention of who said that: Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, he said: Abu 'Asim related to us, he said: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾, he says: the repelling of some of them by others in testimony, in rights, and in what arises from these. He says: were it not for them, these monasteries and what is mentioned with them would have been destroyed.

The most correct of these opinions is that it should be said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, informed that were it not for His repelling people by means of one another, what was mentioned would have been demolished, by His repelling some of them by means of others, and His restraining the polytheists from the Muslims. Among this is His restraining some of them from wronging one another, like a ruler through whom He restrains his subjects from wronging one another; and among this is His restraining, through some of them, those whose testimony is accepted among them from taking away the right of one who has a right against him, and the like. All of that is Allah's repelling of people from one another; were it not for that, they would have wronged one another, and the dominant would have demolished the monasteries and churches of the oppressed and what He, exalted is His praise, named. Allah has not placed in reason any indication that He meant some of that rather than others, nor has any report come that such is the case which must be accepted; so it is according to the apparent and general meaning, as I have already explained, because the general apparent sense includes all that we have mentioned.

* *

His words: ﴿there would have been demolished monasteries﴾

The people of interpretation differed regarding what is meant by the "sawami'" (monasteries). Some of them said: it refers to the monasteries of the monks.

Mention of who said that: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Wahhab related to us, he said: Dawud related to us, from Rafi' regarding this verse: ﴿there would have been demolished monasteries﴾, he said: the monasteries of the monks.

Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, he said: Abu 'Asim related to us, he said: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿there would have been demolished monasteries﴾, he said: the monasteries of the monks.

Al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿there would have been demolished monasteries﴾, he said: the monasteries of the monks.

Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿there would have been demolished monasteries﴾, he said: the monasteries of the monks.

I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words: ﴿there would have been demolished monasteries﴾, and they are the small monasteries which they build [[Probably: "and they are the small monasteries", i.e., small places of worship, etc.]]. Others said: rather, they are the monasteries of the Sabians.

Mention of who said that: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿sawami'﴾, he said: they belong to the Sabians.

al-Hasan related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, the like of it.

The readers differed regarding the recitation of His words: ﴿lahuddimat﴾. The majority of the readers of Madina recited it "lahudimat" with a light (unemphasized) "d." The majority of the readers of Kufa and Basra recited it ﴿lahuddimat﴾ with emphasis (shaddah), meaning the repetition of demolition, one time after another. The emphatic form is more pleasing to me of the two recitations, because such acts are done by the people of disbelief.

As for His words ﴿wa biya'un﴾, it means: the churches of the Christians.

The people of interpretation differed regarding this, and some of them said the same as what we have said.

Mention of who said that: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to me, he said: 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Dawud related to us, from Rafi': ﴿wa biya'un﴾, he said: the churches of the Christians.

Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿wa biya'un﴾, for the Christians.

al-Hasan related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, the like of it.

I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say: al-biya': the churches of the Christians.

Others said: by "bay'" in this place is meant the synagogues of the Jews.

Mention of who said that: Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to us, he said: Abu 'Asim related to us, he said: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, he said: ﴿wa biya'un﴾, he said: and churches.

al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿wa biya'un﴾, he said: the bay' are the churches.

* *

His words: ﴿wa salawat﴾

The people of interpretation differed regarding its meaning. Some of them said: by the "salawat" (prayers) is meant the churches.

Mention of who said that: Muhammad Sa'd related to us, he said: my father related to me, he said: my uncle related to me, he said: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿wa salawat﴾, he said: by the salawat is meant the churches.

I was told from al-Hasan, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words: ﴿wa salawat﴾: the synagogues of the Jews, and they call the synagogue "salawta."

Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿wa salawat﴾: the synagogues of the Jews.

al-Hasan related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, the like of it.

Others said: by the "salawat" is meant the mosques of the Sabians.

Mention of who said that: Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Dawud related to us, he said: I asked Abu al-'Aliya about the salawat. He said: they are the mosques of the Sabians.

He said: 'Abd al-Wahhab related to us, he said: Dawud related to us, from Rafi', similarly.

Others said: they are mosques for the Muslims and for the People of the Book on the roads.

Mention of who said that: Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, he said: Abu 'Asim related to us, he said: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿wa salawat﴾, he said: mosques for the People of the Book and for the people of Islam on the roads.

al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, similarly.

Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿wa salawat﴾, he said: the salawat are the prayers of the people of Islam; when the enemy enters upon them, the worship is cut off, and the mosques are demolished, as Nebuchadnezzar did.

* *

His words: ﴿and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned﴾

The commentators differed regarding the mosques intended by this statement. Some said: what is intended is the mosques of the Muslims.

Mention of who said that: Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Wahhab related to us, he said: Dawud related to us, from Rafi', regarding His words: ﴿wa masajid﴾, he said: the mosques of the Muslims.

Ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, he said: Ibn Thawr related to us, he said: Ma'mar related to us, from Qatada: ﴿and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned﴾, he said: the mosques are the mosques of the Muslims in which the name of Allah is much mentioned.

al-Hasan related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, the like of it.

Others said: by His words ﴿wa masajid﴾ is meant the sawami', the biya', and the salawat.

I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd informed us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿wa masajid﴾: he says, in all of this the name of Allah is much mentioned, and He did not single out the mosques.

Some of the grammarians of Basra used to say: the salawat are not demolished, but it is carried onto another verb, as if he said: "and left salawat." Some said: what is meant is the places of prayer. Others said: they are indeed salawat, and they are the synagogues of the Jews, called in Hebrew "salwta."

The most correct of these opinions is the view of the one who said: the meaning is: monasteries of the monks, churches of the Christians, synagogues of the Jews, which are their houses of worship, and mosques of the Muslims in which the name of Allah is much mentioned.

We held this view to be more correct in interpreting it because it is the known usage in the speech of the Arabs and widespread among them, and what contradicts it, though it may have a valid basis, is not used in the sense intended by the one who intended it.

* *

His words: ﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And Allah will surely help whoever fights in His way, so that His word may be supreme over His enemy. The support of Allah for His servant is His assistance to him, and the support of the servant for his Lord is his striving in His way so that His word may be supreme.

* *

His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, Allah is strong to support those who strive in His way from among the people of His guardianship and obedience, Mighty in His dominion, meaning: unassailable in His authority, no conqueror subdues Him, and no victor overcomes Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 41:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, will establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And with Allah is the outcome of all matters.﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Permission is given to those who are fighting, because they have been wronged, those who, if We establish them in the land, will establish prayer. The words "those who" here are a reference back to "those who are fighting."

By His words ﴿if We establish them in the land﴾ He means: if We settle them in the lands, so that they overpower the polytheists and prevail over them there, and they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). That is, if We give them victory over their enemies and they subdue the polytheists of Mecca, they obey Allah, so they establish the prayer within its limits, and give zakat: that is, they give the zakat of their wealth to those for whom Allah has made it due. ﴿And enjoin what is right﴾: that is, they call people to the oneness of Allah and to acting in obedience to Him, and to what the people of faith in Allah recognise as right. ﴿And forbid what is wrong﴾: that is, they forbid association with Allah and acting in disobedience to Him, which the people of truth and faith in Allah reject. ﴿And with Allah is the outcome of all matters﴾: that is, to Allah belongs the final end of all created beings, meaning that its return is to Him for reward for it and for punishment in the Hereafter.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said in interpreting this.

Those who said this: Al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Husayn al-Ashyab related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far Isa ibn Mahan, who is called al-Razi, related to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, concerning His words ﴿those who, if We establish them in the land, will establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾: He said: Their enjoining of what is right was that they called people to sincerity toward Allah alone, with no partner; and their forbidding of what is wrong was that they forbade the worship of idols and the worship of Satan. He said: Whoever calls people to Allah among all mankind has enjoined what is right, and whoever forbids the worship of idols and the worship of Satan has forbidden what is wrong.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 22, verses 42–45:**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud denied [their messengers] before them, (42) and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot, (43) and the companions of Madyan. And Moses was denied, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them, and how was My rejection!﴾

His words, may His remembrance be exalted, consoling His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) for the harm he suffers from the polytheists, and urging him to be patient with the abuse and denial they direct at him: "And if these polytheists deny you, O Muhammad, for the truth and the proof you have brought them, and for the punishment you warn them of because of their disbelief in God, then this is the way of their brethren from the bygone nations who denied the messengers of God and associated others with Him, and this is their path from before. So let that not hinder you. The humiliating punishment is behind them, and My victory for you and your followers over them is coming to them after that, just as My punishment came upon their forefathers from the nations before them, after a respite until their appointed terms were reached."

"Then the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud denied before them," meaning the Meccan polytheists (the people of Quraysh). "The people of Noah, and ʿAd and Thamud, and the people of Abraham, and the people of Lot, and the companions of Madyan, who are the people of Shuʿayb." He says: all of these denied their messengers. "And Moses was denied." It was said "and Moses was denied" and not "and the people of Moses," because the people of Moses were the Children of Israel, who had responded to him and did not deny him; it was only Pharaoh and his people, the Copts, who denied him.

It has been said: this was said in this form because he was raised among them, just as he was raised among the people of Mecca.

* *

As for His words: ﴿Then I gave the disbelievers respite﴾

He says: I gave respite to the people of disbelief in God among these nations, and did not hasten to them with vengeance and punishment. ﴿Then I seized them﴾ means: then I inflicted punishment upon them after the respite. ﴿And how was My rejection?﴾

He says: So look, O Muhammad, at how My change was, when I altered the blessing they had, and My rejection of them, when I withdrew the kindness I had shown them. Did I not replace their abundance with scarcity, their life with death and destruction, and their prosperity with ruin? He says: So will be My treatment of your deniers from Quraysh, even if I give them respite until their terms. Indeed I will fulfil My promise concerning them, just as I fulfilled My promise concerning others among My messengers and their nations. We destroyed them and saved those who were among them.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed while it was wrongdoing, so it lies in ruins upon its roofs, and [how many] an abandoned well and a lofty castle. (45)﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And how many a town, O Muhammad, have We destroyed while its people were wrongdoers; He says: while they worshipped other than the One who deserves to be worshipped, and disobeyed the One whom they should not have disobeyed.

* *

As for His words: ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs﴾

He says: its people perished and it became empty, emptied of its inhabitants, so it fell into ruin, collapsed and fell down upon its roofs, meaning upon its structures and ceilings.

As related:

- Abu Hisham al-Rifaʿi narrated to us, saying: Abu Khalid narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿so it lies in ruins upon its roofs﴾: he said: its *khawa'* is its ruin, and its *ʿurush* are its ceilings.
- Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿khawiyah﴾: he said: ruined, with no one in it.
- al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

* *

As for His words: ﴿and an abandoned well﴾

And Moses was denied, but I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them, and how was My rejection!﴾

His words, may His remembrance be exalted, consoling His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) for the harm he suffers from the polytheists, and urging him to be patient with the abuse and denial they direct at him: "And if these polytheists deny you, O Muhammad, for the truth and the proof you have brought them, and for the punishment you warn them of because of their disbelief in God, then this is the way of their brethren from the bygone nations who denied the messengers of God and associated others with Him, and this is their path from before. So let that not hinder you. The humiliating punishment is behind them, and My victory for you and your followers over them is coming to them after that, just as My punishment came upon their forefathers from the nations before them, after a respite until their appointed terms were reached."

"Then the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud denied before them," meaning the Meccan polytheists (the people of Quraysh). Some of the scholars of Arabic language interpreted it to mean "adorned with *shid*," from *shadadtuhu ashiduhu* (I adorned it with it), which is similar in meaning to those who said "plastered."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 22, verse 46:

The exegesis of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land, so that they might have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear? For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that grow blind.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Have these deniers of the signs of God and those who reject His power not travelled through the lands, so that they might look upon the places of destruction of their like among those who denied the messengers of God who passed away before them, such as ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Lot and Shuʿayb, and their homelands and dwellings, and so that they might reflect upon them, take warning from them, and know through their contemplation the matter of those places and their people, namely the sunnah (the established way) of God regarding those who disbelieved, worshipped other than Him, and denied His messengers; so that they might turn back (in repentance) from their insolence and disbelief. And it would be for them, if they contemplated that, took warning from it, and turned in repentance to the truth, ﴿hearts with which they understand﴾ the proofs of God upon His creation and His power over what We have explained; ﴿or ears with which they hear﴾, meaning: or ears that listen to the hearing of the truth, so that they comprehend it and distinguish between it and falsehood.

* *

As for His words: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind﴾

He means: their eyes do not become blind so that they cannot see with them the persons and behold them; rather they see those things with their eyes. But their hearts, which are within their breasts, grow blind to the helpers of the truth and to knowing it.

The hāʾ in His words ﴿fa-innahā lā taʿmā﴾ is a hāʾ of ʿimād (a dummy or anticipatory pronoun), like the speaker's saying: "innahu ʿabdullāhi qāʾimun" (indeed, it is ʿAbdullah who is standing).

It has been mentioned that in the recitation of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) it reads: "fa-innahu lā taʿmā al-abṣāru". It is said that ﴿but it is the hearts within the breasts that grow blind﴾ is stated, since hearts are only ever within the breasts, as emphasis for the speech, just as it is said: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾.

**The commentary on His words, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will never fail to fulfil His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ (22:47)**

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: O Muhammad, the polytheists of your people ask you to hasten the punishment of Allah that you threaten them with, for their polytheism and their denial of you regarding what you brought them from Allah in this world. But Allah will not fail to fulfil His promise, which He made to you concerning them, of sending down His punishment and vengeance upon them in the immediate world. He did so, and He fulfilled for them what He had promised them, and so He killed them on the day of Badr.

The people of ta'wil (interpretation of meaning) differed about the day that He, may His majesty be praised, mentioned: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾. Which day is it? Some of them said: It is one of the days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth.

Mention of those who said that: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, he said: Israʾil narrated to us, from Simak, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: "It is from the days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord﴾ ... the verse, he said: "It is like His words in 'Alif Lam Mim, Tanzil', exactly the same; it is the same verse."

Others said: Rather, it is from the days of the Hereafter.

Mention of those who said that: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Hakkam narrated to us, from ʿAnbasa, from Simak, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The measure of the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection is a thousand years."

Yaʿqub narrated to me, he said: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, he said: Saʿid al-Juraybiri narrated to us, from Abu Nadrah, from Samir ibn Nahar, who said: Abu Hurayrah said: "The poor among the Muslims will enter Paradise before the rich by a measure of half a day." I said: "And what is half a day?" He said: "Do you not recite the Qur'an?" I said: "Yes." He said: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to me, he said: Abu ʿAwanah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Mujahid: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾, he said: "It is from the days of the Hereafter."

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, he said: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Simak, from ʿIkrimah, that he said regarding this verse: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾, he said: "These are the days of the Hereafter." And regarding His words: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [70:4], he said: "It is the Day of Resurrection." And he recited: ﴿They see it as far off, but We see it as near﴾ [70:6–7].

The interpretation has differed as to the direction of the speech, from the report about those who sought to hasten the punishment, to the report about the length of a day in the sight of Allah. Some of them said: The people sought to hasten the punishment in this world, so Allah revealed: ﴿But Allah will not fail to fulfil His promise﴾ concerning sending down what He had promised them of punishment in this world. And [the meaning of] ﴿indeed, a day with your Lord﴾ is that His punishment of them, in this world and the Hereafter, is like a thousand years of what you count in this world.

Others said: It was said in this manner to inform those who sought the punishment hastily that He does not hasten, but gives respite until a term He has appointed; and that what seems slow to them is near to Him. So He said to them: The measure of a day with Me is a thousand years of what you, O people, count of your days; it seems slow to you, but near to Me.

Others said: The meaning of that is: ﴿And indeed, a day﴾ of heaviness and fear is like a thousand years.

The second view is, in my opinion, closer to the truth in this matter. This is because Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, informed of the polytheists' seeking to hasten the punishment for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then informed of the extent of the measure of a day with Him, and then followed that with His words: ﴿And how many a town did I give respite while it was wrongdoing﴾ [22:48]. So He reported about His giving respite to the people of the wrongdoing town, leaving off hastening their punishment. Thereby He made clear that by His words ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ He intended to negate hastiness from Himself, and to describe Himself with patience and waiting. Since that is the case, the interpretation of the speech is: Indeed, a day among the days that are with Allah is the Day of Resurrection, one day being like a thousand years of your counting; it is not far in His sight, though it is far in yours. Therefore He does not hasten the punishment of whoever He wishes to punish until he reaches the end of his term.

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿And how many a town have I given respite while it was wrongdoing; then I seized it, and to Me is the destination﴾ [22:48].

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿And how many a town have I given respite﴾ — meaning: I granted them respite and deferred their punishment, while they were associating others with God and opposing His command. That was the wrongdoing by which God described them, may His praise be exalted. So I did not hasten their punishment. ﴿Then I seized it﴾ — meaning: then I seized it with punishment, punishing it in this world by bringing down Our retribution upon them. ﴿And to Me is the destination﴾ — meaning: their destination is also to Me after their destruction, so they will then encounter a punishment that has no end. God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: thus is the case of those among your idolatrous people who seek to hasten punishment. Even if I give them respite until their appointed terms that I have set for them, I will surely seize them with punishment. Fight them with the sword, and then their destination is to Me; so I will cause them pain then, as a retribution for the sins they committed.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿Say: O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you. So those who believed and did righteous deeds — for them is forgiveness and noble provision. And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate [them] — those are the companions of Hellfire﴾ [22:49–51].

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Say, O Muhammad, to the idolaters of your people who dispute with you about God without knowledge, following every rebellious devil: ﴿O mankind, I am only a clear warner to you﴾ — I warn you of God's punishment descending upon you in this world, and of His torment in the Hereafter that you will burn in, clearly; meaning: I make my warning to you plain and manifest, so that you may repent of your polytheism and beware of what I warn you of. I have no power over anything for you beyond that. As for hastening or delaying the punishment with which you urge me, that rests with God, not with me, and I have no power over it. Then He described his warning and his good tidings, though no mention of good tidings had preceded; and since the warning was mentioned with a specific action, it is understood that the good tidings are its opposite. So He said: those who believed in God and His Messenger and did righteous deeds, among you, O people, and among others — ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾ — meaning: for them, from God, is the covering of the sins they committed in this world, so that they are concealed from them in the Hereafter; ﴿and noble provision﴾ — meaning: a goodly provision in Paradise.

As related:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, regarding His words: ﴿So those who believed and did righteous deeds — for them is forgiveness and noble provision﴾ — he said: Paradise.

* *

And His words: ﴿And those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate [them]﴾

Meaning: those who worked against Our proofs, turning people away from following Our Messenger and from acknowledging Our Book which We sent down. He said "against Our signs," and the preposition "fi" (in/against) is used here as in the expression "so-and-so strove in the matter of so-and-so."

The exegetes differed on the interpretation of His words ﴿mu'ajjizin﴾ (seeking to frustrate). Some of them said: its meaning is "opposing" (mushaqqin).

Those who said this: Ahmad ibn Yusuf narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Uthman ibn 'Ata', from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he recited it as ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ throughout the Qur'an, meaning with an alif, and said: opposing.

Others said: rather, the meaning is that they thought they could overcome God, so that He could not prevail over them.

Those who said this: Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿against Our signs, seeking to frustrate﴾ — he said: they denied God's signs and thought they could overcome God, but they will never overcome Him.

⁕ al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, the like of it.

These two interpretations are based on the reading of those who recite it ﴿mu'ajizin﴾ with an alif, which is the common reading of the reciters of Medina and Kufa. As for some reciters of Mecca and Basra, they read it "mu'ajjizin" with a doubled jim and without an alif, meaning that they rendered people incapable and deterred them from following the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and believing in the Qur'an.

Those who interpreted it in accordance with this reading: Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words "mu'ajjizin," he said: those who slow people down, slowing them from following the Prophet (ﷺ).

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

The correct position on this matter is to say that both are well-known readings, each recited by scholars among the reciters, and their meanings are close. For whoever is incapable regarding God's signs has effectively been incapable before God, and to strive against God is to render people incapable of God's signs and to act in disobedience to Him and in opposition to His command. The people about whom these verses were revealed were of the kind who slowed people down from faith in God and following His Messenger, and who contended against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), supposing that they could frustrate and overcome him, while God had guaranteed him victory over them; that was their striving against God. Given this, whichever of the two readings the reciter uses, he is correct.

As for "mu'ajaza," it is the form of mufa'ala from "ajz" (incapacity), and its meaning is the contest of two parties, each seeking to render the other incapable, so that one overcomes and subdues the other.

As for "ta'jiz," it is the intensive form, the tafil form of "ajz."
